  • Distinguer dans un cahier des charges les exigences obligatoires (shall / must) des exigences souhaitables (should / may) sans erreur sur 5 exigences.
  • Identifier dans un appel d'offres les critères d'attribution, leur pondération, l'échéance de remise et les motifs d'exclusion.
  • Repérer dans un avis de clarification ce qui modifie ou ne modifie pas le dossier initial.

Compétence C2 — niveau B2.2 — 50 min

Un appel d'offres (invitation to tender, ITT ; request for proposal, RFP ; request for quotation, RFQ pour une simple demande de prix) et son cahier des charges (specification, statement of requirements, terms of reference) sont des documents contractuels. Chaque mot compte : une erreur de lecture peut exclure une offre.

1. Le vocabulaire de l'obligation. C'est le point décisif :

  • shall / must / is required to = exigence obligatoire (mandatory requirement) ; une offre qui ne la respecte pas est écartée (non-compliant) ;
  • should / is preferred / is desirable = exigence souhaitable, qui rapporte des points mais n'est pas éliminatoire ;
  • may = option laissée au soumissionnaire ;
  • shall not / must not = interdiction.

Une question type B2 : « Which of the following is optional? » La bonne réponse se trouve dans une phrase avec may ou desirable.

2. La structure d'un dossier. On y trouve : le contexte (background), l'objet (scope of work), les exigences techniques, les livrables (deliverables), le calendrier (timeline), les modalités de remise (submission requirements), les critères d'attribution (award criteria) avec leur pondération (weighting), et les motifs d'exclusion.

3. Les critères d'attribution. Le marché n'est pas toujours attribué au moins cher : the contract will be awarded to the most economically advantageous tender signifie que la qualité technique, le délai ou le service après-vente comptent aussi. Lisez les pourcentages : technical merit 50%, price 30%, after-sales service 20%.

4. Les dates. Distinguez la date limite de questions (deadline for clarification questions), la date limite de remise (closing date, submission deadline), la date d'attribution (award date) et la date de démarrage. Une offre reçue après la date limite est en général refusée (late submissions will not be considered).

5. Les avis de clarification et avenants. Un clarification notice répond aux questions des soumissionnaires ; un addendum modifie le dossier. Repérez les formules remains unchanged (inchangé), is hereby amended (est modifié), supersedes (remplace).

6. Les conditions et réserves. Subject to (sous réserve de), unless otherwise agreed (sauf accord contraire), at the bidder's own expense (aux frais du soumissionnaire), including but not limited to (notamment, liste non exhaustive).

Méthode : surlignez mentalement tous les shall/must, notez chaque date avec ce à quoi elle correspond, et vérifiez la pondération avant de juger ce qui « compte le plus ».

Langue clé

AnglaisFrançaisUsage
The supplier shall provide on-site training for all users.Le fournisseur devra assurer une formation sur site pour tous les utilisateurs.exigence obligatoire
Remote diagnostics capability is desirable but not mandatory.Une capacité de diagnostic à distance est souhaitable mais non obligatoire.exigence souhaitable
Bidders may submit an alternative solution.Les soumissionnaires peuvent présenter une variante.option
The contract will be awarded to the most economically advantageous tender.Le marché sera attribué à l'offre économiquement la plus avantageuse.critère d'attribution global
Late submissions will not be considered.Les offres hors délai ne seront pas examinées.motif d'exclusion
Section 4.2 is hereby amended as follows…La section 4.2 est modifiée comme suit…avenant modifiant le dossier

Vocabulaire

TermeTraductionExemple
invitation to tender (ITT)appel d'offresThe college has issued an invitation to tender for training simulators.
specificationcahier des charges, spécification techniqueThe technical specification is attached as Annex B.
bidder / tenderersoumissionnaireEach bidder may submit only one tender.
mandatory requirementexigence obligatoireFailure to meet a mandatory requirement leads to exclusion.
award criteriacritères d'attributionThe award criteria are listed in Section 6.
weightingpondérationPrice has a weighting of 30%.
compliantconformeOnly compliant tenders will be evaluated.
closing datedate limite de remiseThe closing date is 12 noon on 3 November.
clarification noticeavis de clarificationA clarification notice has been published on the portal.
addendumavenant, additif au dossierAddendum 1 supersedes the original timeline.
to supersederemplacer, annuler et remplacerThis version supersedes all previous versions.
warrantygarantieA minimum three-year warranty is required.
lead timedélai de livraison, délai d'approvisionnementPlease state the lead time for spare parts.
subject tosous réserve deThe award is subject to budget approval.

Dialogue : Décortiquer un appel d'offres avant de répondre

Bureau d'un fabricant de bancs de formation électrique. Une ingénieure commerciale et un acheteur-chef de projet analysent un appel d'offres reçu d'un établissement d'enseignement.

PersonnageRépliqueTraduction
Anika BrandtSamuel, the Ashgrove tender closes on the third of November. Before we decide to bid, let's check the mandatory requirements.Samuel, l'appel d'offres d'Ashgrove se clôture le 3 novembre. Avant de décider de répondre, vérifions les exigences obligatoires.
Samuel OtienoI've highlighted every 'shall' in the specification. There are eleven.J'ai surligné chaque « shall » du cahier des charges. Il y en a onze.
Anika BrandtAny we can't meet?Y en a-t-il que nous ne pouvons pas respecter ?
Samuel OtienoJust one worries me: 'The supplier shall guarantee spare parts availability for ten years.' Our standard commitment is seven.Une seule m'inquiète : « Le fournisseur devra garantir la disponibilité des pièces pendant dix ans. » Notre engagement standard est de sept ans.
Anika BrandtThen that's a question for the clarification stage. The deadline for questions is the twentieth, isn't it?Alors c'est une question pour la phase de clarification. La date limite des questions, c'est le 20, non ?
Samuel OtienoYes, the twentieth of October. The closing date is two weeks later.Oui, le 20 octobre. La date de remise est deux semaines plus tard.
Anika BrandtAnd remote diagnostics? Our competitors don't offer it.Et le diagnostic à distance ? Nos concurrents ne le proposent pas.
Samuel OtienoIt's listed as 'desirable', so it isn't compulsory, but it should earn us points under technical merit.Il est indiqué comme « souhaitable », donc pas obligatoire, mais il devrait nous rapporter des points sur la valeur technique.
Anika BrandtGood. How is the score weighted?Bien. Comment la note est-elle pondérée ?
Samuel OtienoTechnical merit fifty per cent, price thirty, after-sales service twenty.Valeur technique cinquante pour cent, prix trente, service après-vente vingt.
Anika BrandtSo we don't have to be the cheapest. Quality counts for more than price here.Donc nous n'avons pas besoin d'être les moins chers. Ici, la qualité compte plus que le prix.
Samuel OtienoExactly. But if we miss a single mandatory requirement, the technical score won't even be calculated.Exactement. Mais si nous manquons une seule exigence obligatoire, la note technique ne sera même pas calculée.
Anika BrandtRight. Draft the clarification question on spare parts today, and I'll prepare the compliance matrix.D'accord. Rédige aujourd'hui la question de clarification sur les pièces, et je prépare la matrice de conformité.

Exercices corrigés

Exercice 1 — B2-M3-L3-I1 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cet extrait d'appel d'offres puis répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

ASHGROVE COLLEGE – INVITATION TO TENDER
Reference: AC-ITT-2026-14
Supply of electrical installation training benches

  1. Background

Ashgrove College is expanding its electrical engineering workshop to accommodate apprentices from three regional employers. The College wishes to purchase twelve training benches allowing learners to practise domestic and industrial wiring in safe, low-voltage conditions.

  1. Scope

The contract covers the supply, installation and commissioning of the benches, initial training for teaching staff, and maintenance for a period of three years from acceptance. Furniture and IT equipment are outside the scope of this tender.

  1. Key requirements

3.1 The benches shall comply with current electrical safety standards for teaching environments.
3.2 The supplier shall deliver and install all benches before 15 January, as the first cohort begins on 2 February.
3.3 The supplier shall provide at least one full day of on-site training for up to six members of staff.
3.4 A remote diagnostics function is desirable.
3.5 Bidders may propose an extended warranty as a priced option.

  1. Award criteria

The contract will be awarded to the most economically advantageous tender, assessed as follows: technical merit 50%; price 30%; after-sales service 20%. Tenders that fail to meet any requirement in 3.1 to 3.3 will be considered non-compliant and will not be scored.

  1. Submission

Clarification questions must be sent through the procurement portal no later than 20 October. Responses will be published to all bidders without identifying the sender. Tenders must be uploaded by 12 noon on 3 November. Late submissions will not be considered. The College reserves the right not to award the contract if no tender represents value for money.

1. Which of the following is NOT included in the contract?
A. Training for teaching staff
B. Three years of maintenance
C. Furniture for the workshop
D. Commissioning of the benches

2. Why is the installation deadline important to the College?
A. A new group of learners starts soon after.
B. The college's budget expires on 15 January.
C. The warranty period begins on 2 February.
D. Employers will inspect the workshop in January.

3. What would happen to a tender that does not offer remote diagnostics?
A. It would be excluded as non-compliant.
B. It would be accepted only with an extended warranty.
C. It would have to be resubmitted before 3 November.
D. It could be scored but lose technical points.

4. What does the College say about clarification questions?
A. They must be sent by email to the head of the workshop.
B. The answers will be shared with every bidder anonymously.
C. They can be submitted until the closing date.
D. Only bidders who ask questions will receive the answers.

Corrigé

1. C — Furniture for the workshop. « Furniture and IT equipment are outside the scope of this tender ». La formation, la maintenance et la mise en service figurent toutes dans la section 2.
2. A — A new group of learners starts soon after.. « before 15 January, as the first cohort begins on 2 February » : « as » donne la raison. Aucune expiration de budget ni inspection n'est mentionnée.
3. D — It could be scored but lose technical points.. Le diagnostic à distance est « desirable » (3.4), donc non éliminatoire. Seules les exigences 3.1 à 3.3 rendent une offre non conforme : l'option 1 est le piège principal.
4. B — The answers will be shared with every bidder anonymously.. « Responses will be published to all bidders without identifying the sender ». La date limite des questions (20 octobre) est antérieure à la date de remise (3 novembre) : l'option 3 confond les deux.

Exercice 2 — B2-M3-L3-I2 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cet extrait de cahier des charges technique et répondez aux questions.

Delmont Foods – Statement of Requirements
Project: Replacement of the conveyor system, Chilled Distribution Centre, Unit 4

  1. Objective

The current conveyor line, installed in 2009, can no longer handle peak volumes, and unplanned stoppages have increased steadily over the past two years. Delmont Foods intends to replace it with a system able to process 2,400 cases per hour, with the possibility of extending capacity to 3,000 cases per hour at a later stage without replacing the main structure.

  1. Operating conditions

The system shall operate continuously at an ambient temperature of 2 to 4°C. All components in contact with packaging shall be suitable for use in a food environment and easy to clean. Noise levels should not exceed 70 dB at a distance of one metre; proposals that achieve lower levels will be viewed favourably.

  1. Installation constraints

The distribution centre operates seven days a week. Installation work shall therefore be carried out in phases, and at no point shall more than one of the three loading zones be out of service. The contractor may propose night work, provided that it is included in the fixed price.

  1. Documentation and training

The contractor shall supply operating manuals in English and Polish, reflecting the language needs of our staff. Training should be delivered on site, on each of the three shifts, so that no team is excluded.

  1. Performance guarantee

Acceptance will be subject to a 30-day performance test. If the system fails to reach the required throughput during this period, Delmont Foods reserves the right to withhold 15% of the contract value until the issue is resolved.

1. What does Delmont Foods want regarding future capacity?
A. The system must process 3,000 cases per hour from the start.
B. Capacity must be expandable without a new main structure.
C. The old structure must be reused for the new system.
D. Capacity will be reviewed after the performance test.

2. Which requirement is NOT strictly mandatory?
A. Operating at 2 to 4°C
B. Food-safe, easy-to-clean components
C. Manuals in English and Polish
D. A noise level of 70 dB or less

3. Under what condition can the contractor work at night?
A. If it does not increase the agreed price
B. If two loading zones remain closed
C. If staff on all three shifts agree
D. If the installation falls behind schedule

4. What happens if the system does not reach the required throughput during the test?
A. The contract is automatically cancelled.
B. The contractor must install a second line.
C. Part of the payment can be withheld until it is fixed.
D. Delmont Foods will extend the test to 60 days at its own cost.

Corrigé

1. B — Capacity must be expandable without a new main structure.. « with the possibility of extending capacity to 3,000 cases per hour at a later stage without replacing the main structure ». 3 000 caisses/heure est une capacité future, pas une exigence initiale (option 1).
2. D — A noise level of 70 dB or less. Le bruit est introduit par « should not exceed » et les niveaux plus bas sont « viewed favourably » : c'est une exigence souhaitable. Les trois autres sont introduites par « shall ».
3. A — If it does not increase the agreed price. « The contractor may propose night work, provided that it is included in the fixed price ». L'option 2 contredit la règle : jamais plus d'une zone hors service.
4. C — Part of the payment can be withheld until it is fixed.. « Delmont Foods reserves the right to withhold 15% of the contract value until the issue is resolved » = retenir une partie du paiement. Aucune résiliation automatique n'est prévue (option 1).

Exercice 3 — B2-M3-L3-I3 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cet avis de clarification publié pendant une consultation et répondez aux questions.

LUMERA BIOSCIENCES – PROCUREMENT DEPARTMENT
RFP LB-2026-07: Laboratory waste collection and disposal services
Clarification Notice No. 2 – issued 9 October

This notice responds to questions received from bidders up to 6 October. It forms part of the tender documents. Except where expressly stated below, all other provisions of the RFP remain unchanged.

Q1. Can bidders subcontract the transport of hazardous chemical waste?
A1. Yes, subcontracting of transport is permitted, provided that the subcontractor holds the relevant licence and is named in the tender. The prime contractor remains fully responsible for compliance. Subcontracting of the final treatment of waste is not permitted.

Q2. The RFP requires weekly collection from all three sites. Would fortnightly collection be acceptable for the Hillcrest site, which produces smaller volumes?
A2. Weekly collection remains a requirement for all sites. However, bidders may submit a priced variant with fortnightly collection at Hillcrest. Variants will only be considered if the main offer is compliant.

Q3. Section 7 states that the contract will start on 1 January. Is this date fixed?
A3. No. Following a delay in internal approvals, Section 7 is hereby amended: the contract start date is now 1 March. The closing date for tenders is not affected and remains 31 October.

Q4. Will Lumera provide historical waste volumes by category?
A4. A summary table covering the last 24 months has been uploaded to the portal as Annex F. Please note that the figures for the current year are provisional.

Bidders are reminded that no further questions will be accepted after 16 October.

1. What does the notice say about the rest of the RFP?
A. It has been withdrawn and will be reissued.
B. It still applies unless this notice changes it.
C. It is replaced entirely by this notice.
D. It applies only to the Hillcrest site.

2. Which activity must NOT be subcontracted?
A. The final treatment of the waste
B. The transport of hazardous chemical waste
C. Weekly collection at Hillcrest
D. Licence checks on transport companies

3. What is the status of fortnightly collection at Hillcrest?
A. It replaces weekly collection at that site from the start.
B. It is forbidden in all circumstances.
C. It may be offered as a variant to a compliant offer.
D. It will be decided after the contract start date.

4. Which date has been changed by this notice?
A. The closing date for tenders
B. The deadline for questions
C. The date of the summary table
D. The start date of the contract

Corrigé

1. B — It still applies unless this notice changes it.. « Except where expressly stated below, all other provisions of the RFP remain unchanged ». L'avis complète le dossier, il ne le remplace pas (option 3).
2. A — The final treatment of the waste. « Subcontracting of the final treatment of waste is not permitted ». Le transport peut être sous-traité sous conditions (option 2).
3. C — It may be offered as a variant to a compliant offer.. « Weekly collection remains a requirement… bidders may submit a priced variant… Variants will only be considered if the main offer is compliant ». L'option 1 est le contresens : la collecte hebdomadaire reste obligatoire.
4. D — The start date of the contract. « Section 7 is hereby amended: the contract start date is now 1 March. The closing date… is not affected ». « hereby amended » signale la modification.

Exercice 4 — B2-M3-L3-I4 (C2, B2.2)

Complétez cet extrait de dossier de consultation avec le terme exact.

All [1] _____ must submit their offers via the portal. Any offer that fails to meet a mandatory requirement will be considered non-[2] _____. Price carries a [3] _____ of 30%. This version [4] _____ the document issued on 2 September. The award remains [5] _____ to the approval of the governing board. Bidders shall state the [6] _____ time for spare parts.

[1] bidders / biddings / offerers / tendered

[2] conform / compliant / complying / accordant

[3] weight / weighing / weighting / balance

[4] supersedes / succeeds / overpasses / overrides to

[5] submitted / subject / subjected / subordinate

[6] lead / leading / delivering / lag

Corrigé

[1] bidders. « bidders » = soumissionnaires. « offerers » n'existe pas dans ce sens ; « tendered » est un participe.
[2] compliant. « non-compliant » = non conforme. « conform » est un verbe, pas un adjectif.
[3] weighting. « weighting » = pondération d'un critère. « weighing » est la pesée.
[4] supersedes. « supersedes » = annule et remplace une version antérieure. « succeeds » signifie « vient après », sans annuler la précédente.
[5] subject. « subject to » = sous réserve de. « subjected to » signifie « soumis à (un traitement) ».
[6] lead. « lead time » = délai d'approvisionnement ou de livraison.

title: B2-M3 — Articles de presse économique : point de vue, nuance, argumentation
description: Formuler en une phrase la thèse d'un article économique de 300 mots après une seule lecture. Identifier les concessions, contre-arguments et réserves de l'auteur à partir des connecteurs (admittedly, while, yet, that said). Distinguer l'opinion de l'auteur de celle des personnes qu'il cite, grâce aux verbes introducteurs (claim, argue, concede, dismiss).
imageQuery: business English Articles de presse économique : point de vue, nuance, argumentation

sections.title: B2-M3-L4 — Articles de presse économique : point de vue, nuance, argumentation
sections.contentHtml:
Objectifs :

  • Formuler en une phrase la thèse d'un article économique de 300 mots après une seule lecture.
  • Identifier les concessions, contre-arguments et réserves de l'auteur à partir des connecteurs (admittedly, while, yet, that said).
  • Distinguer l'opinion de l'auteur de celle des personnes qu'il cite, grâce aux verbes introducteurs (claim, argue, concede, dismiss).

Compétence C2 — niveau B2.2 — 50 min

Un article de presse économique ne se contente pas d'informer : il défend une position, souvent de façon nuancée. Les questions de niveau B2 portent sur la thèse, les concessions et l'attitude de l'auteur.

1. Trouver la thèse. Elle apparaît en général à la fin de l'introduction ou dans la conclusion : The real question is not whether…, but…, What this shows is that…, The lesson for managers is clear…. Le titre peut être ironique ou provocateur : ne le prenez pas pour la thèse sans vérifier.

2. Repérer les concessions. Un auteur nuancé reconnaît les arguments adverses avant de les dépasser :

  • Admittedly / Granted / It is true that… (certes) ;
  • While / Although / Even though… (bien que) ;
  • That said / Nonetheless / Yet / Still (cela dit, pourtant).

La structure « concession + but/yet + position » est la plus fréquente : Admittedly, the four-day week has its critics. Yet the evidence so far is encouraging. La position de l'auteur est après le connecteur d'opposition.

3. Distinguer les voix. Un article cite des experts, des dirigeants, des syndicats. Le verbe introducteur indique l'attitude de l'auteur envers la personne citée :

  • neutre : say, state, explain ;
  • distance : claim, insist, maintain (prétendre, affirmer sans preuve) ;
  • accord : point out, rightly note, show ;
  • rejet : dismiss, play down (balayer, minimiser) ;
  • concession : concede, acknowledge, admit.

Une opinion citée n'est pas forcément celle de l'auteur : Supporters claim that… annonce souvent une réserve.

4. Lire l'attitude. Les adjectifs et adverbes évaluatifs trahissent la position : surprisingly, worryingly, predictably, a welcome step, a costly mistake, overstated. Les guillemets autour d'un mot (the so-called « revolution ») marquent souvent l'ironie ou la distance.

5. Les modaux de prudence. This could mean…, may well…, it would be premature to… montrent que l'auteur ne tire pas de conclusion définitive. Une option qui présente comme certain ce que l'auteur dit « possible » est fausse.

Méthode : après la première lecture, résumez la thèse en une phrase ; notez les connecteurs de concession ; pour chaque citation, demandez-vous si l'auteur l'approuve, la nuance ou la rejette.

Langue clé

AnglaisFrançaisUsage
Admittedly, the policy has its critics. Yet the early results are encouraging.Certes, la mesure a ses détracteurs. Pourtant, les premiers résultats sont encourageants.concession suivie de la position de l'auteur
The real question is not whether…, but how…La vraie question n'est pas de savoir si…, mais comment…annoncer la thèse
Supporters claim that costs will fall, but the evidence is thin.Les partisans affirment que les coûts baisseront, mais les preuves sont minces.prendre ses distances avec une opinion citée
She rightly points out that…Elle souligne à juste titre que…approuver une opinion citée
It would be premature to conclude that…Il serait prématuré de conclure que…nuancer, éviter une conclusion hâtive
That said, the risks should not be dismissed.Cela dit, les risques ne doivent pas être balayés.introduire une réserve

Vocabulaire

TermeTraductionExemple
reshoringrelocalisation (de la production)Reshoring has become a political priority.
supply chainchaîne d'approvisionnementThe crisis exposed fragile supply chains.
admittedlycertes, il faut le reconnaîtreAdmittedly, labour costs are higher in Europe.
to concedeconcéder, reconnaîtreThe CEO conceded that the targets were ambitious.
to dismissrejeter, balayer (une idée)Economists dismissed the claim as unrealistic.
to play downminimiserThe firm played down the impact of the strike.
productivity gainsgains de productivitéThe productivity gains have not yet materialised.
staff turnoverrotation du personnelStaff turnover fell by a third.
evidencepreuves, données probantes (indénombrable)The evidence so far is mixed.
prematureprématuréIt is premature to call the trial a success.
spin-offentreprise issue d'un laboratoire, essaimageThe university has created twelve spin-offs.
single-sourcingapprovisionnement auprès d'un fournisseur uniqueSingle-sourcing reduces costs but increases risk.
trade-offcompromis, arbitrageThere is a trade-off between cost and resilience.
so-calledsoi-disant, prétenduThe so-called revolution has been slow to arrive.

Dialogue : Revue de presse du lundi matin

Équipe achats d'un groupe industriel, réunion hebdomadaire. Un acheteur présente un article économique et sa collègue l'aide à dégager la position de l'auteur.

PersonnageRépliqueTraduction
Rachel AdeyemiDiego, you wanted to share an article on reshoring?Diego, tu voulais partager un article sur la relocalisation ?
Diego MarchettiYes. The headline is 'The factory comes home', so I assumed it was enthusiastic about reshoring.Oui. Le titre est « L'usine rentre à la maison », donc j'ai supposé qu'il était enthousiaste sur la relocalisation.
Rachel AdeyemiAnd is it?Et c'est le cas ?
Diego MarchettiNot really. The author admits that some companies have brought production back, but then says the trend is much smaller than politicians claim.Pas vraiment. L'auteur reconnaît que certaines entreprises ont rapatrié leur production, mais dit ensuite que la tendance est bien plus faible que ne le prétendent les politiques.
Rachel AdeyemiNotice the verb 'claim'. It tells you the journalist doesn't fully believe them.Remarque le verbe « claim ». Il montre que le journaliste ne les croit pas vraiment.
Diego MarchettiRight. And there's a quote from an economist who says reshoring is mostly about automation, not jobs.C'est vrai. Et il y a une citation d'un économiste qui dit que la relocalisation concerne surtout l'automatisation, pas l'emploi.
Rachel AdeyemiDoes the author agree with her?L'auteur est-il d'accord avec elle ?
Diego MarchettiYes, he writes that she 'rightly points out' the gap. So that's his view too.Oui, il écrit qu'elle « souligne à juste titre » l'écart. C'est donc aussi son avis.
Rachel AdeyemiSo what's the thesis in one sentence?Alors, quelle est la thèse en une phrase ?
Diego MarchettiThat companies aren't really bringing factories home; they're diversifying suppliers to reduce risk.Que les entreprises ne rapatrient pas vraiment leurs usines ; elles diversifient leurs fournisseurs pour réduire les risques.
Rachel AdeyemiWhich is exactly what we're doing with our castings. Does he see any downside?C'est exactement ce que nous faisons pour nos pièces de fonderie. Voit-il un inconvénient ?
Diego MarchettiHe concedes that diversification costs more in the short term, but he argues it's a price worth paying.Il concède que la diversification coûte plus cher à court terme, mais il soutient que c'est un prix qui vaut la peine d'être payé.
Rachel AdeyemiGood summary. Concession, then position. Can you circulate the article with your one-line summary?Bon résumé. Concession, puis position. Peux-tu diffuser l'article avec ton résumé en une ligne ?
Diego MarchettiI'll send it this afternoon.Je l'envoie cet après-midi.

Exercices corrigés

Exercice 1 — B2-M3-L4-I1 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cet article de presse économique puis répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

The factory comes home – or does it?

Few economic ideas have enjoyed such political popularity in recent years as reshoring. After a series of supply-chain shocks, ministers across Europe have promised to bring production back from distant suppliers, and a handful of well-publicised factory openings have been presented as proof that the trend is under way.

Admittedly, some firms have indeed moved production closer to home. Surveys of manufacturers show that around one in five has relocated at least part of its activity over the past five years. Yet the scale of the movement is far smaller than politicians claim. Imports of manufactured goods from outside Europe have barely fallen, and in several sectors they have continued to rise.

What is happening, in fact, is something more subtle. Rather than closing factories in Asia, many companies are adding a second or third supplier in a different region, so that a single disruption cannot stop production altogether. Procurement specialists call this the shift from 'just in time' to 'just in case'.

The employment benefits are also more modest than promised. As Professor Ingrid Solberg of the Northern Institute of Industrial Economics rightly points out, the factories that do return are often highly automated. 'A plant that once employed 800 people abroad may come back with 150,' she notes.

None of this means that reshoring is a myth. Diversification has a real cost: dual sourcing typically raises purchasing costs by several percentage points, and smaller firms may struggle to absorb it. That said, the events of recent years suggest that it is a price worth paying. The real question for managers is not whether to bring everything home, but how much resilience they are prepared to buy.

1. How does the author present the factory openings mentioned in the first paragraph?
A. As clear evidence of a major economic shift
B. As politicians' evidence for their argument
C. As the result of new European subsidies
D. As proof that imports from Asia have fallen

2. What is the function of the sentence beginning 'Yet the scale of the movement…'?
A. It gives the author's reservation after a concession.
B. It summarises the results of the manufacturers' survey.
C. It explains why imports have increased.
D. It repeats the politicians' argument.

3. According to the article, what are many companies actually doing?
A. Closing their factories in Asia
B. Buying exclusively from European suppliers
C. Adding suppliers in other regions to spread risk
D. Returning to 'just in time' production

4. What is the author's overall position?
A. Reshoring is a myth invented by politicians.
B. Diversification is too expensive for most firms.
C. Companies should bring all production back home.
D. Building resilience costs money but is justified.

Corrigé

1. B — As politicians' evidence for their argument. Les ouvertures d'usines « have been presented as proof » par les responsables politiques : la tournure passive marque une distance. L'auteur ne les considère pas lui-même comme une preuve (option 1).
2. A — It gives the author's reservation after a concession.. Structure « Admittedly… Yet… » : l'auteur concède un fait (des entreprises ont relocalisé) puis exprime sa réserve (le phénomène est bien plus limité). Le verbe « claim » marque sa distance envers les politiques (option 4).
3. C — Adding suppliers in other regions to spread risk. « many companies are adding a second or third supplier in a different region ». Le texte précise « Rather than closing factories in Asia », ce qui écarte l'option 1.
4. D — Building resilience costs money but is justified.. « That said, the events of recent years suggest that it is a price worth paying ». L'auteur écrit explicitement « None of this means that reshoring is a myth », ce qui exclut l'option 1.

Exercice 2 — B2-M3-L4-I2 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cette tribune parue dans une revue professionnelle d'ingénierie et répondez aux questions.

Opinion – Is the four-day week ready for engineering?
by Tomasz Wierzbicki

When Kestrel Design Partners, a 140-person structural engineering consultancy, announced last year that its staff would work four days a week for the same salary, many in the industry predicted chaos. Clients, they said, would not tolerate slower responses, and project deadlines would slip.

Twelve months on, the firm's figures make interesting reading. Staff turnover has fallen by a third, sick leave is down, and the number of job applications has tripled. Its managing director, Claire Odum, insists that productivity has 'at least held steady'. Billable hours, however, have fallen by 6%, and the firm concedes that some large projects have needed weekend cover from a rota of volunteers.

It would be easy to dismiss the experiment as a perk that only a profitable firm can afford. That would be a mistake. Engineering consultancies are struggling to recruit, and a policy that triples applications deserves to be taken seriously. Equally, though, it would be premature to present Kestrel as a model for the whole sector. Its clients are mainly private developers who are relatively flexible about meeting times; firms working on public infrastructure, with strict reporting obligations, may find the arrangement far harder to manage.

What the Kestrel case really shows is that working time can be redesigned, but not simply reduced. The firm cut internal meetings by half and introduced 'focus mornings' without email before it shortened the week. Those changes, rather than the extra day off in itself, are probably what made the policy work. Firms tempted to copy the four-day week should start there.

1. What did many people in the industry expect when the policy was announced?
A. That clients would leave and deadlines slip
B. That staff would refuse to work weekends
C. That salaries would be reduced to cover the cost
D. That job applications would fall

2. What does the word 'insists' suggest about the managing director's claim?
A. It is fully supported by the figures quoted.
B. The author treats it with some caution.
C. It was made against the board's wishes.
D. It refers only to job applications.

3. Why does the author think Kestrel should not be seen as a model for every firm?
A. Its staff turnover was already very low.
B. Its profits fell sharply during the year.
C. Its clients are unusually flexible.
D. Its volunteers refused to continue the weekend rota.

4. According to the author, what made the policy successful?
A. The extra day off itself
B. Higher salaries for all staff
C. The support of private developers
D. Earlier changes to how work was organised

Corrigé

1. A — That clients would leave and deadlines slip. « many in the industry predicted chaos. Clients… would not tolerate slower responses, and project deadlines would slip ». Les salaires sont maintenus (« for the same salary »), ce qui écarte l'option 3.
2. B — The author treats it with some caution.. « insists » marque une affirmation appuyée mais non démontrée ; la phrase suivante (« Billable hours, however, have fallen by 6% ») nuance d'ailleurs cette affirmation. L'option 1 ignore ce « however ».
3. C — Its clients are unusually flexible.. « Its clients are mainly private developers who are relatively flexible… firms working on public infrastructure… may find the arrangement far harder to manage ». Rien n'indique une chute des bénéfices (option 2).
4. D — Earlier changes to how work was organised. « Those changes [moins de réunions, matinées sans email], rather than the extra day off in itself, are probably what made the policy work ». « rather than » écarte explicitement l'option 1.

Exercice 3 — B2-M3-L4-I3 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cet article sur les partenariats entre universités et entreprises et répondez aux questions.

Labs and profits: an uneasy partnership

Universities are under growing pressure to show that their research produces economic value. Governments now routinely measure them by the number of patents filed, spin-off companies created and contracts signed with industry. The University of Marbury, which has launched twelve spin-offs in five years, is often held up as an example of what this approach can achieve.

The benefits are real. Industrial partners bring funding, equipment and practical problems that can lead to unexpected discoveries. Students who work on industry projects are, according to several studies, more likely to find skilled jobs quickly. And for companies, access to university expertise is far cheaper than building their own research teams.

Yet the model has drawbacks that its supporters tend to play down. Researchers at Marbury report spending a growing share of their time negotiating contracts and confidentiality agreements rather than doing research. Some fear that subjects with no obvious commercial application, such as fundamental physics or the history of science, will gradually lose funding. Dr Hamid Rezaei, who leads a materials science group, puts it bluntly: 'We are starting to choose questions according to who will pay for the answers.'

None of this argues for closing the door to industry. The most successful partnerships, as a recent review of thirty projects shows, are those in which the university keeps control of the research agenda and companies fund broad programmes rather than individual results. Policymakers would do well to reward that kind of partnership instead of simply counting spin-offs.

1. How is the University of Marbury presented in the first paragraph?
A. As a university that refuses to work with industry
B. As a frequently cited success story
C. As the institution that created the government's measures
D. As a university facing financial difficulties

2. What does the author suggest about the supporters of the model?
A. They exaggerate the cost of university research.
B. They are mainly students looking for jobs.
C. They tend to minimise its disadvantages.
D. They want to close universities to industry.

3. What is Dr Rezaei's concern?
A. Research priorities are being shaped by funding sources.
B. Companies are refusing to sign confidentiality agreements.
C. His group lacks modern equipment.
D. Students are leaving for industry too early.

4. What does the author recommend to policymakers?
A. Increasing the number of spin-offs
B. Reducing industry funding for universities
C. Funding fundamental physics instead of industrial projects
D. Rewarding partnerships where universities keep control

Corrigé

1. B — As a frequently cited success story. « is often held up as an example of what this approach can achieve » = est souvent cité en exemple. Aucune difficulté financière n'est évoquée.
2. C — They tend to minimise its disadvantages.. « drawbacks that its supporters tend to play down » : « to play down » = minimiser. L'option 4 correspond à une position que l'auteur rejette lui-même plus loin.
3. A — Research priorities are being shaped by funding sources.. « We are starting to choose questions according to who will pay for the answers » : les financeurs orientent les sujets de recherche. Les accords de confidentialité prennent du temps, mais personne ne refuse de les signer (option 2).
4. D — Rewarding partnerships where universities keep control. « Policymakers would do well to reward that kind of partnership instead of simply counting spin-offs » (celui où l'université garde la maîtrise du programme). L'option 1 est précisément ce que l'auteur critique.

Exercice 4 — B2-M3-L4-I4 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cet article de la presse spécialisée achats et répondez aux questions.

The hidden cost of the cheapest supplier

For decades, purchasing departments were judged on a simple measure: how much money they saved. Buyers who negotiated the lowest unit price were rewarded, and single-sourcing, which concentrates volumes on one supplier in exchange for a discount, was considered best practice.

That logic is now being questioned, and not only because of recent disruptions. A study of 200 mid-sized manufacturers published this spring found that firms relying on a single supplier for critical components suffered, on average, three times as many days of halted production as those using two or more. The researchers estimate that, once lost sales and emergency freight are included, the apparent savings of single-sourcing disappeared within two years in most cases.

Some procurement directors remain unconvinced. 'Dual sourcing doubles the administrative work and dilutes our negotiating power,' argues Fiona Mallory, head of purchasing at a packaging group. She has a point: managing two suppliers means two audits, two quality agreements and smaller volumes for each. For low-value, easily replaceable items, the case for a second supplier is weak.

The lesson, then, is not that single-sourcing should be abandoned, but that it should be reserved for parts whose failure would not stop production. Increasingly, the most advanced purchasing teams classify components according to risk as well as cost, and set different strategies for each category. Measuring buyers on savings alone, however, encourages exactly the opposite behaviour. Until performance indicators change, it would be naive to expect purchasing practices to change with them.

1. According to the study, what happened to the savings from single-sourcing?
A. They increased over time.
B. They were usually wiped out by disruption costs.
C. They were reinvested in qualifying a second supplier.
D. They were three times higher than expected.

2. How does the author respond to Fiona Mallory's argument?
A. He partly accepts it for certain types of item.
B. He rejects it as outdated.
C. He considers it proof that dual sourcing always fails.
D. He says it applies only to packaging groups.

3. Why does the author believe purchasing practices may not change quickly?
A. Suppliers refuse to sign quality agreements.
B. Dual sourcing is illegal for critical parts.
C. Buyers are still evaluated mainly on cost savings.
D. Most manufacturers have not read the study.

Corrigé

1. B — They were usually wiped out by disruption costs.. « once lost sales and emergency freight are included, the apparent savings… disappeared within two years in most cases ». « three times » concerne les jours d'arrêt de production (option 4).
2. A — He partly accepts it for certain types of item.. « She has a point… For low-value, easily replaceable items, the case for a second supplier is weak » : l'auteur lui donne partiellement raison. Il ne la rejette pas (option 1).
3. C — Buyers are still evaluated mainly on cost savings.. « Measuring buyers on savings alone… encourages exactly the opposite behaviour. Until performance indicators change, it would be naive to expect purchasing practices to change ». Aucune des autres raisons n'est mentionnée.

Exercice 5 — B2-M3-L4-I5 (C2, B2.2)

Complétez ce paragraphe d'article avec le connecteur ou le verbe introducteur qui convient.

[1] _____, the new tariff policy has helped some local producers. [2] _____, most economists remain sceptical. The minister [3] _____ that prices will fall within a year, but she offers little evidence. Industry leaders, for their part, have [4] _____ the risk of shortages, describing it as 'manageable'. It would be [5] _____ to judge the policy after only six months.

[1] Admittedly / Consequently / Furthermore / Otherwise

[2] Therefore / Nevertheless / Similarly / In addition

[3] claims / concedes / denies / admits

[4] pointed out / played down / raised / highlighted

[5] premature / precocious / previous / preliminary

Corrigé

[1] Admittedly. « Admittedly » (certes) introduit une concession, suivie ici d'une opposition. « Consequently » exprimerait une conséquence, sans lien logique avec la phrase précédente.
[2] Nevertheless. « Nevertheless » (néanmoins) marque l'opposition après la concession. « Therefore » annoncerait une conséquence, ce qui contredit le sens.
[3] claims. « claims » = affirme (sans preuve), cohérent avec « but she offers little evidence ». « concedes » signifierait qu'elle reconnaît un point défavorable.
[4] played down. « played down » = minimisé, cohérent avec « describing it as manageable ». « highlighted » signifierait au contraire « mis en avant ».
[5] premature. « It would be premature to… » = il serait prématuré de… « precocious » (précoce) s'emploie pour un enfant ou un talent, pas pour un jugement.

title: B2-M3 — Correspondance délicate : réclamation et négociation par écrit
description: Identifier dans une réclamation écrite la demande réelle de l'émetteur, distincte des griefs qu'il exprime. Repérer dans un échange de négociation les concessions proposées et les conditions dont elles dépendent (provided that, on condition that, unless). Qualifier le ton d'un courrier délicat (ferme, conciliant, menaçant, diplomatique) en s'appuyant sur au moins deux indices lexicaux.
imageQuery: business English Correspondance délicate : réclamation et négociation par écrit

sections.title: B2-M3-L5 — Correspondance délicate : réclamation et négociation par écrit
sections.contentHtml:
Objectifs :

  • Identifier dans une réclamation écrite la demande réelle de l'émetteur, distincte des griefs qu'il exprime.
  • Repérer dans un échange de négociation les concessions proposées et les conditions dont elles dépendent (provided that, on condition that, unless).
  • Qualifier le ton d'un courrier délicat (ferme, conciliant, menaçant, diplomatique) en s'appuyant sur au moins deux indices lexicaux.

Compétence C2 — niveau B2.2 — 45 min

La correspondance délicate — réclamation, contestation de facture, renégociation de prix — est rarement directe. L'émetteur reste courtois, mais chaque phrase est pesée. Lire ces messages au niveau B2, c'est lire entre les lignes.

1. Séparer griefs et demande. Une réclamation contient souvent plusieurs reproches (the delivery was late, the parts were damaged, nobody answered our calls), mais une seule demande principale : remplacement, avoir (credit note), remise, pénalité, engagement écrit. Cherchez les formules we therefore expect / we would ask you to / we request that… : la demande suit généralement le mot therefore.

2. Les adoucisseurs (softeners). Le registre diplomatique atténue la critique : We were somewhat surprised… (nous avons été assez surpris = mécontents) ; It appears that… (il semble que…) ; We would appreciate it if… ; Unfortunately, we are not in a position to… (nous ne pouvons pas = refus). Un refus poli reste un refus.

3. Les marqueurs de fermeté. Ils signalent une escalade : This is the third time this year…, We must insist…, We reserve the right to… (menace voilée : pénalités, résiliation), Failing this, we will have no choice but to…, without prejudice (sans reconnaissance de responsabilité). La présence de dates précises et de références contractuelles (under clause 8.2) montre que l'émetteur prépare un éventuel litige.

4. La négociation écrite. Repérez :

  • la position de départ (our standard price is…) ;
  • la concession (we are prepared to / we could consider / as a gesture of goodwill) ;
  • la condition (provided that, on condition that, as long as, subject to) ;
  • la limite (this is our final offer, we cannot go below…).

Une concession conditionnelle n'est pas acquise : si la condition n'est pas remplie, l'offre tombe. Les QCM jouent souvent sur cet oubli.

5. Reconnaître sans admettre. Les fournisseurs écrivent volontiers We regret any inconvenience caused (sans reconnaître de faute) plutôt que We apologise for our mistake (reconnaissance de responsabilité). La nuance compte pour la suite du dossier.

Méthode : soulignez la demande, encadrez chaque condition, notez la date limite et classez le ton sur une échelle de 1 (conciliant) à 4 (pré-contentieux) en justifiant par deux mots du texte.

Langue clé

AnglaisFrançaisUsage
We were somewhat surprised to receive an invoice for…Nous avons été assez surpris de recevoir une facture pour…exprimer un mécontentement de façon atténuée
We therefore request that you issue a credit note.Nous vous demandons donc d'émettre un avoir.formuler la demande principale
We reserve the right to apply the penalties set out in clause 8.Nous nous réservons le droit d'appliquer les pénalités prévues à l'article 8.menace voilée, escalade
As a gesture of goodwill, we are prepared to offer a 5% discount.À titre de geste commercial, nous sommes disposés à accorder une remise de 5 %.faire une concession
This offer is conditional on a two-year commitment.Cette offre est subordonnée à un engagement de deux ans.poser une condition
Unfortunately, we are not in a position to accept this proposal.Malheureusement, nous ne sommes pas en mesure d'accepter cette proposition.refus poli

Vocabulaire

TermeTraductionExemple
credit noteavoirPlease issue a credit note for the damaged items.
grievancegrief, sujet de mécontentementThe letter lists three grievances.
gesture of goodwillgeste commercialAs a gesture of goodwill, we will waive the delivery charge.
to waiverenoncer à, annuler (des frais)We are prepared to waive the late-payment fee.
penalty clauseclause de pénalitéThe contract includes a penalty clause for late delivery.
to escalatefaire remonter, porter à un niveau supérieurWe will escalate the matter to our legal department.
without prejudicesous toutes réserves, sans reconnaissance de responsabilitéThis offer is made without prejudice.
price adjustmentrévision de prixThe supplier requested a price adjustment of 8%.
to absorb (a cost)absorber, prendre à sa chargeWe cannot absorb the full increase.
counter-proposalcontre-propositionPlease find our counter-proposal below.
to fall short ofne pas atteindre, être en deçà deThe service fell short of our expectations.
invoice disputecontestation de factureThe invoice dispute was resolved in a week.
bindingcontraignant, fermeThis quotation is binding for 60 days.

Dialogue : Répondre à une réclamation sans perdre le client

Service clients d'un fabricant de composants hydrauliques. Une responsable grands comptes analyse avec son directeur l'email d'un client mécontent avant d'y répondre.

PersonnageRépliqueTraduction
Sophie AchterbergNeil, we've had a rather sharp email from Brackwater Logistics about the valve order.Neil, nous avons reçu un email assez sec de Brackwater Logistics au sujet de la commande de vannes.
Neil FairbanksHow sharp? Are they threatening to cancel?Sec à quel point ? Menacent-ils d'annuler ?
Sophie AchterbergNot directly. But they write 'this is the third late delivery this year' and 'we reserve the right to apply the penalty clause'.Pas directement. Mais ils écrivent « c'est la troisième livraison en retard cette année » et « nous nous réservons le droit d'appliquer la clause de pénalité ».
Neil FairbanksThat's a warning shot. What exactly are they asking for?C'est un coup de semonce. Que demandent-ils exactement ?
Sophie AchterbergThat's the interesting part. After all the complaints, the actual request is a written recovery plan by Friday.C'est ça qui est intéressant. Après toutes les plaintes, la demande réelle est un plan de rattrapage écrit d'ici vendredi.
Neil FairbanksSo they want reassurance, not money. At least for now.Donc ils veulent être rassurés, pas de l'argent. Du moins pour l'instant.
Sophie AchterbergExactly. If the plan is convincing, I don't think they'll escalate.Exactement. Si le plan est convaincant, je ne pense pas qu'ils iront plus loin.
Neil FairbanksBe careful with the wording. Don't write 'we apologise for our mistake'. Part of the delay was caused by their late drawings.Fais attention à la formulation. N'écris pas « nous nous excusons pour notre erreur ». Une partie du retard vient de leurs plans transmis en retard.
Sophie AchterbergI'll say 'we sincerely regret the disruption caused' and then set out the facts.J'écrirai « nous regrettons sincèrement la gêne occasionnée » puis j'exposerai les faits.
Neil FairbanksGood. Can we offer something as a gesture of goodwill?Bien. Pouvons-nous proposer quelque chose à titre de geste commercial ?
Sophie AchterbergWe could waive the express freight charges on the next two orders, provided they confirm the volumes for the next quarter.Nous pourrions renoncer aux frais de transport express sur les deux prochaines commandes, à condition qu'ils confirment les volumes du prochain trimestre.
Neil FairbanksA concession with a condition. That's fine. Send me the draft before it goes out.Une concession avec une condition. Ça me va. Envoie-moi le brouillon avant de l'expédier.
Sophie AchterbergYou'll have it within the hour.Tu l'auras dans l'heure.

Exercices corrigés

Exercice 1 — B2-M3-L5-I1 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cette réclamation d'un client puis répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

From: Gareth Pryce <g.pryce@brackwater-logistics.example>
To: Sophie Achterberg <s.achterberg@kessler-hydraulics.example>
Cc: Procurement Director, Brackwater Logistics
Subject: Order KH-55281 – repeated delivery failures

Dear Ms Achterberg,

I am writing regarding order KH-55281 for 340 hydraulic control valves, which was due for delivery to our Rotterdam depot on 22 September and arrived, incomplete, on 1 October.

I regret to say that this is the third late delivery this year. On this occasion, the delay forced us to keep two of our automated sorting lines on reduced capacity for six working days. In addition, 28 of the valves received show visible damage to the connectors, apparently caused by inadequate packaging. Our technicians have set these aside and they will not be installed.

I appreciate that your team informed us of the delay, and I am aware that our revised drawings reached you a few days later than planned. However, your confirmation of 4 September already took those drawings into account, and the date you confirmed was not met.

I would therefore ask you to send us, by Friday 10 October, a written recovery plan setting out (1) a firm delivery date for the 52 missing valves, (2) the replacement of the 28 damaged units at no cost to us, and (3) the measures you will take to prevent a recurrence, including any changes to packaging.

I should add that, under clause 9.3 of our framework agreement, we are entitled to apply a penalty of 0.5% of the order value per day of delay. We reserve the right to do so, but our preference at this stage is to find a constructive solution.

I look forward to your reply.

Yours sincerely,
Gareth Pryce
Operations Manager, Brackwater Logistics

1. What was the main operational consequence of the late delivery for Brackwater?
A. Two sorting lines had to run below full capacity.
B. The Rotterdam depot was closed for six days.
C. Technicians had to repair the damaged valves.
D. The revised drawings had to be sent again.

2. Why does Mr Pryce mention the confirmation of 4 September?
A. To show that the drawings were sent on time
B. To accept that Brackwater was partly responsible for the delay
C. To prevent Kessler from blaming the late drawings
D. To ask for a new confirmation of the order

3. What does Mr Pryce actually request?
A. Immediate payment of the penalty
B. Cancellation of the remaining part of the order
C. A discount on the next three orders
D. A written plan to fix the problems

4. How would you describe the tone of the final paragraph?
A. Openly aggressive and final, with no room for discussion
B. Firm, with a warning, but open to a solution
C. Apologetic and uncertain
D. Friendly and informal

Corrigé

1. A — Two sorting lines had to run below full capacity.. « the delay forced us to keep two of our automated sorting lines on reduced capacity for six working days ». Les vannes endommagées ne sont pas réparées mais mises de côté (option 3).
2. C — To prevent Kessler from blaming the late drawings. Il reconnaît le retard des plans, puis précise que la confirmation du 4 septembre en tenait déjà compte : l'argument des plans ne peut donc plus justifier le retard. L'option 2 est tentante, mais il désamorce justement cette responsabilité.
3. D — A written plan to fix the problems. « I would therefore ask you to send us… a written recovery plan setting out (1)… (2)… (3)… ». La pénalité n'est qu'une possibilité (« we reserve the right »), pas la demande.
4. B — Firm, with a warning, but open to a solution. « We reserve the right to do so » (avertissement) + « our preference at this stage is to find a constructive solution » (ouverture). Le ton est ferme sans être définitif : l'option 1 ignore la seconde moitié de la phrase.

Exercice 2 — B2-M3-L5-I2 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cette réponse d'un fournisseur dans une négociation de prix et répondez aux questions.

From: Martin Haugland <m.haugland@nordcast-components.example>
To: Rachel Adeyemi <r.adeyemi@halvorsen-pumps.example>
Subject: RE: Proposed price adjustment 2027 – castings

Dear Rachel,

Thank you for your message of 2 October and for the open discussion we had last week. I fully understand that an increase of 9% on our cast iron housings is difficult for Halvorsen to accept at a time when your own customers are resisting price rises.

As I explained, the increase reflects higher energy and alloy costs, which have risen by well over 9% since our last adjustment two years ago. We have already absorbed part of this increase ourselves, and we are not in a position to absorb more without compromising our investment in the new moulding line.

That said, we value our partnership and have looked carefully at your counter-proposal. Unfortunately, a freeze on prices until the end of 2027 is not something we can consider. We could, however, offer the following:

  • an increase limited to 6%, provided that Halvorsen commits to a minimum annual volume of 18,000 units for two years;
  • payment terms of 45 days instead of the current 30, which would ease your cash flow;
  • quarterly reviews, so that the price can be reduced if energy costs fall by more than 10%.

If the volume commitment is not possible, our original proposal of 9% would apply, although we would still be willing to discuss the payment terms.

Please note that this offer is valid until 31 October, as we need to finalise our energy contracts for next year.

Kind regards,
Martin Haugland
Sales Director, Nordcast Components

1. Why does Mr Haugland say he cannot absorb more of the cost increase?
A. His customers are resisting price rises.
B. He needs to protect his investment in new equipment.
C. His energy contracts have already been signed.
D. Halvorsen has reduced its order volumes.

2. What was Halvorsen's counter-proposal?
A. A 6% increase
B. Payment terms of 45 days
C. A price freeze until the end of 2027
D. A minimum volume commitment for two years

3. Under what condition would the increase be limited to 6%?
A. If energy costs fall by more than 10%
B. If Halvorsen accepts payment terms of 45 days
C. If Halvorsen replies before 31 October
D. If Halvorsen commits to a two-year volume

4. What would happen if Halvorsen could not commit to the volume?
A. The 9% rise would apply, with terms still negotiable.
B. Nordcast would end the partnership.
C. The 6% offer would remain valid after the 31 October deadline.
D. Prices would be frozen until the end of 2027.

Corrigé

1. B — He needs to protect his investment in new equipment.. « we are not in a position to absorb more without compromising our investment in the new moulding line ». La résistance des clients concerne ceux de Halvorsen (option 1), pas les siens.
2. C — A price freeze until the end of 2027. « a freeze on prices until the end of 2027 is not something we can consider » : c'était la contre-proposition de Halvorsen, que Nordcast refuse. Les 6 % sont l'offre de Nordcast.
3. D — If Halvorsen commits to a two-year volume. « an increase limited to 6%, provided that Halvorsen commits to a minimum annual volume of 18,000 units for two years ». La baisse liée à l'énergie (option 1) relève des révisions trimestrielles.
4. A — The 9% rise would apply, with terms still negotiable.. « our original proposal of 9% would apply, although we would still be willing to discuss the payment terms ». Rien n'indique une rupture du partenariat, au contraire (« we value our partnership »).

Exercice 3 — B2-M3-L5-I3 (C2, B2.2)

Lisez cette contestation de facture adressée à un organisme de formation et répondez aux questions.

From: Dr Helen Achebe, Principal, Westbridge Technical School
To: Accounts Department, Ridgeview Learning Services
Subject: Invoice RLS-2026-0412 – disputed amount

Dear Sir or Madam,

We have received your invoice RLS-2026-0412 for £14,600 relating to the staff training programme on digital assessment delivered in September. While we were generally satisfied with the quality of the sessions, I am afraid we cannot pay the invoice in its current form.

Our agreement, signed in June, provided for six on-site days at £2,100 per day, giving a total of £12,600. Your invoice includes an additional £2,000 described as 'preparation and travel'. We were somewhat surprised to see this item, as the agreement clearly states that the daily rate is all-inclusive. Moreover, the sixth session, scheduled for 26 September, was cancelled by your trainer on the morning itself, and it has not yet been rescheduled.

We are therefore willing to pay £10,500 now, corresponding to the five days actually delivered. The balance of £2,100 will be paid once the sixth session has taken place, provided that it is held before the end of November, when our staff will need the training for the first assessment period.

I would be grateful if you could issue a corrected invoice on this basis. For the avoidance of doubt, we would like to continue working with Ridgeview next year, and I hope this matter can be settled quickly and amicably.

Yours faithfully,
Dr Helen Achebe

1. Why does Dr Achebe dispute the 'preparation and travel' charge?
A. The sessions were of poor quality.
B. The trainer did not travel to the school.
C. The agreed daily rate already covered such costs.
D. The charge was higher than in the previous year.

2. How much does the school agree to pay immediately?
A. £14,600
B. £12,600
C. £2,100
D. £10,500

3. What does the final paragraph suggest about the school's intentions?
A. It wants to resolve the dispute and maintain the relationship.
B. It intends to take legal action if the invoice is not corrected.
C. It will look for another training provider next year.
D. It refuses to pay anything until November.

Corrigé

1. C — The agreed daily rate already covered such costs.. « the agreement clearly states that the daily rate is all-inclusive ». Elle précise au contraire être globalement satisfaite de la qualité (option 1).
2. D — £10,500. « We are therefore willing to pay £10,500 now, corresponding to the five days actually delivered ». 12 600 £ est le total prévu au contrat pour six jours.
3. A — It wants to resolve the dispute and maintain the relationship.. « we would like to continue working with Ridgeview next year, and I hope this matter can be settled quickly and amicably ». Aucune action en justice n'est évoquée ; l'école paie d'ailleurs une partie immédiatement (option 4).

Exercice 4 — B2-M3-L5-I4 (C2, B2.2)

Complétez cette réponse diplomatique à une réclamation avec le terme exact.

Dear Mr Pryce,

Thank you for your email. We sincerely [1] _____ the disruption caused to your operations. As a gesture of [2] _____, we will replace the damaged units and [3] _____ the express freight charges on your next two orders, [4] _____ that the volumes for Q1 are confirmed by 20 October. Please note that this offer is made without [5] _____ to our position under the framework agreement. A corrected delivery schedule is attached; it is [6] _____ for both parties once you have confirmed it.

Kind regards,
Sophie Achterberg

[1] regret / apologise / excuse / deplore for

[2] goodness / goodwill / good faith / kindness

[3] waive / wave / avoid / release

[4] provided / unless / despite / even

[5] prejudice / prejudgement / preference / precedence

[6] bound / binding / bonded / bounding

Corrigé

[1] regret. « We sincerely regret the disruption » : regret + complément direct, sans reconnaissance de faute. « apologise » exigerait « for » (« apologise for the disruption »).
[2] goodwill. Expression figée : « a gesture of goodwill » (geste commercial).
[3] waive. « to waive a charge » = renoncer à facturer des frais. « wave » (faire signe) est un homophone piège.
[4] provided. « provided that » = à condition que : la concession dépend de la confirmation des volumes. « unless » inverserait la condition.
[5] prejudice. « without prejudice » = sans reconnaissance de responsabilité, sous toutes réserves.
[6] binding. « binding » = contraignant, qui engage. « bound » s'emploie avec un sujet personne : « we are bound by the schedule ».

title: B2-M3 — Classe virtuelle : lecture rapide et stratégique
description: Dégager en 90 secondes l'objet, la thèse ou la demande principale d'un document de 300 mots par lecture globale. Répondre à 4 questions sur un document de 300 mots en moins de 6 minutes en ciblant la zone du texte utile à chaque question. Justifier oralement chaque réponse en citant le passage exact et en expliquant pourquoi le distracteur le plus proche est faux.
imageQuery: business English Classe virtuelle : lecture rapide et stratégique

sections.title: B2-M3-L6 — Classe virtuelle : lecture rapide et stratégique
sections.contentHtml:
Objectifs :

  • Dégager en 90 secondes l'objet, la thèse ou la demande principale d'un document de 300 mots par lecture globale.
  • Répondre à 4 questions sur un document de 300 mots en moins de 6 minutes en ciblant la zone du texte utile à chaque question.
  • Justifier oralement chaque réponse en citant le passage exact et en expliquant pourquoi le distracteur le plus proche est faux.

Compétence C2 — niveau B2.2 — 30 min — classe virtuelle

Au niveau B2, la difficulté n'est plus de comprendre chaque phrase, mais de lire vite sans perdre la nuance. Le référentiel le formule ainsi : comprendre des contenus professionnels « en adaptant sa vitesse de lecture aux textes, situations et objectifs ». Cette classe virtuelle entraîne trois vitesses de lecture.

1. Lecture d'orientation (30 à 90 secondes). Avant les questions, parcourez : titre ou objet, première et dernière phrase de chaque paragraphe, mots en gras, chiffres et noms propres. Objectif : savoir de quel type de document il s'agit (rapport, appel d'offres, article d'opinion, réclamation) et où se trouve chaque bloc d'information. Formulez mentalement : This is a … in which … argues / asks / reports that ….

2. Lecture ciblée (scanning). Lisez la question, puis identifiez le type d'information attendu :

  • un fait chiffré → cherchez les chiffres ;
  • une cause → cherchez because, due to, driven by, as ;
  • une condition → provided that, unless, only if ;
  • une opinion → in our view, rightly, claim, however ;
  • une demande → we would ask, please, we therefore request.

Comme les questions suivent l'ordre du texte, la réponse à la question 3 se trouve après celle de la question 2.

3. Lecture fine (close reading). Une fois la zone repérée, ralentissez et lisez la phrase entière et la suivante. C'est là que se cachent les nuances : un however qui renverse le sens, un partly qui limite une cause, un could qui transforme un fait en possibilité, une négation (not yet, no longer, rather than).

Gérer son temps. Pour un document de 300 mots et 4 questions, visez : 1 minute d'orientation, 1 minute par question, 1 minute de vérification. Si vous hésitez entre deux options, éliminez celle qui :

  • reprend des mots exacts du texte mais dans une autre relation logique ;
  • généralise (always, all, every) ce que le texte limite ;
  • attribue l'action à la mauvaise personne.

Pendant la séance, vous travaillerez en temps limité, seul puis en sous-groupe, et vous devrez toujours citer la phrase du texte qui justifie votre choix, en anglais.

Langue clé

AnglaisFrançaisUsage
This is a memo in which the author asks for…Il s'agit d'une note dans laquelle l'auteur demande…résumer un document après la lecture d'orientation
The answer is in the third paragraph, where it says…La réponse se trouve au troisième paragraphe, où il est dit…justifier sa réponse à l'oral
Option B is tempting, but the text says 'partly', not 'mainly'.L'option B est tentante, mais le texte dit « en partie », pas « principalement ».expliquer pourquoi un distracteur est faux
The key word here is 'however'.Le mot-clé ici est « however ».signaler une nuance décisive
The author doesn't say it will happen, only that it could.L'auteur ne dit pas que cela arrivera, seulement que cela pourrait arriver.distinguer certitude et possibilité

Vocabulaire

TermeTraductionExemple
to skimparcourir, lire en diagonaleSkim the text before reading the questions.
to scanbalayer du regard (pour trouver une information)Scan the report for the closing date.
close readinglecture attentive, lecture fineThe last question requires close reading.
gistidée générale, l'essentielI got the gist of the article in one minute.
key wordmot-cléUnderline the key words in each question.
distractordistracteur (option piège)The distractor repeats words from the text.
to rule outéliminer, écarterWe can rule out option C immediately.
paraphrasereformulationThe correct option is usually a paraphrase of the text.
time budgettemps allouéSet yourself a time budget of six minutes.
to back upétayer, justifierBack up your answer with a quotation.

Dialogue : Six minutes pour un document

Classe virtuelle. La formatrice lance un défi chronométré et deux apprenants comparent leurs stratégies de lecture.

PersonnageRépliqueTraduction
Claire Dumont-HaleRight, everyone. You have six minutes for this document and four questions. Before you start, how will you use the first minute?Bien, tout le monde. Vous avez six minutes pour ce document et quatre questions. Avant de commencer, comment allez-vous utiliser la première minute ?
Yusuf DemirI'll skim it: the subject line, the first sentence of each paragraph and the last paragraph.Je vais le parcourir : l'objet, la première phrase de chaque paragraphe et le dernier paragraphe.
Claire Dumont-HaleGood. And then?Bien. Et ensuite ?
Lena HartmannThen I read the first question and decide what I'm looking for: a number, a reason, a condition or an opinion.Ensuite je lis la première question et je décide ce que je cherche : un chiffre, une raison, une condition ou une opinion.
Claire Dumont-HaleExactly. Off you go. … Time's up. Yusuf, question two. What did you choose?Exactement. C'est parti. … Temps écoulé. Yusuf, question deux. Qu'as-tu choisi ?
Yusuf DemirI chose B, that the delay was caused by the supplier.J'ai choisi B, que le retard était dû au fournisseur.
Claire Dumont-HaleCan you back that up with the text?Peux-tu justifier avec le texte ?
Yusuf DemirHmm. The text says the delay was 'partly explained by' the supplier. So it's not the only reason.Hum. Le texte dit que le retard est « en partie expliqué » par le fournisseur. Donc ce n'est pas la seule raison.
Lena HartmannThat's why I chose C. The next sentence says the main cause was the staff shortage.C'est pour ça que j'ai choisi C. La phrase suivante dit que la cause principale était le manque de personnel.
Claire Dumont-HaleWell spotted, Lena. Always read the sentence after the one you find. That's where the nuance often is.Bien vu, Lena. Lisez toujours la phrase qui suit celle que vous trouvez. C'est souvent là qu'est la nuance.
Yusuf DemirSo B was a distractor: it uses words from the text, but changes the logic.Donc B était un distracteur : il reprend des mots du texte, mais change la logique.
Claire Dumont-HalePrecisely. Now, in your breakout rooms, do the same with the article. Six minutes again.Précisément. Maintenant, dans vos salles de sous-groupe, faites la même chose avec l'article. Six minutes à nouveau.

Déroulé de la classe virtuelle

  1. 3 min — Accueil, objectifs de la séance, rappel des trois vitesses de lecture (orientation, ciblage, lecture fine).
  2. 8 min — Défi individuel chronométré sur B2-M3-L6-I1 (6 min), puis correction collective : chaque réponse est justifiée par une citation en anglais.
  3. 10 min — Salles de sous-groupe (3 apprenants) sur B2-M3-L6-I2 : 6 min de lecture, puis 4 min pour se mettre d'accord et préparer l'explication du distracteur le plus tentant.
  4. 6 min — Mise en commun : chaque groupe présente une question ; le formateur note au tableau partagé les pièges rencontrés (partly / mainly, rather than, could, concessions).
  5. 3 min — Bilan : chaque apprenant formule sa règle personnelle de gestion du temps ; consigne de la mise en pratique du module et de l'exercice B2-M3-L6-I3.

Exercices corrigés

Exercice 1 — B2-M3-L6-I1 (C2, B2.2)

Défi chronométré (6 minutes) : lisez cette note interne et répondez aux questions. Préparez la citation qui justifie chaque réponse.

MEMO
To: All project managers, Corvane Engineering
From: Laura Petrenko, Director of Engineering
Subject: Project documentation – new review procedure from 1 November

Over the past year, our clients have raised concerns about the quality of the technical documentation we deliver at the end of projects. An internal audit of 40 recent projects confirmed that the problem is real, though perhaps less serious than some complaints suggested: most documents were technically accurate, but one in four was delivered late, and many were difficult to navigate because each team used its own format.

To address this, the following procedure will apply to all projects starting on or after 1 November. Projects already under way are not affected, although project managers are encouraged to apply the new templates where this does not cause delays.

  1. All final documentation must use the standard templates available on the intranet.
  2. A peer review by an engineer from another team is required before any document is sent to the client.
  3. The documentation schedule must be included in the project plan from the start, rather than being prepared in the final weeks.

I am aware that the peer review will add work at a time when teams are already busy. To limit the impact, reviewers will be able to record up to four hours per review as billable time on the project, and we will monitor the workload over the first three months. If the procedure proves too heavy, we will adjust it.

Please send any questions or suggestions to the Quality Office before 24 October, so that we can include answers in the FAQ that will be published with the templates.

1. What did the internal audit find?
A. Most documents contained technical errors.
B. Documents were accurate but often late or unclear.
C. Client complaints were entirely unjustified and exaggerated.
D. Only four projects had documentation problems.

2. Which projects must follow the new procedure?
A. All projects, including those already under way
B. Only projects with documentation problems
C. Projects that start on or after 1 November
D. Projects selected by the Quality Office

3. How does the director respond to concerns about extra workload?
A. Review time is billable and workload will be monitored.
B. Peer reviews will be optional during the first three months.
C. Each team will review its own documents to save time.
D. Additional engineers will be recruited for reviews.

4. Why should questions be sent before 24 October?
A. Because the templates will be withdrawn after that date
B. Because the audit results will be published then
C. Because the procedure starts on 24 October
D. So that the answers can be included in a published FAQ

Corrigé

1. B — Documents were accurate but often late or unclear.. « most documents were technically accurate, but one in four was delivered late, and many were difficult to navigate ». L'option 1 contredit « technically accurate » ; l'option 3 contredit « the problem is real ».
2. C — Projects that start on or after 1 November. « will apply to all projects starting on or after 1 November. Projects already under way are not affected » ; pour ceux-ci, les modèles sont seulement encouragés (option 1).
3. A — Review time is billable and workload will be monitored.. « reviewers will be able to record up to four hours per review as billable time… and we will monitor the workload over the first three months ». La relecture par un ingénieur d'une autre équipe est obligatoire dès le départ : les options 2 et 3 sont donc fausses.
4. D — So that the answers can be included in a published FAQ. « before 24 October, so that we can include answers in the FAQ » : « so that » introduit le but. La procédure démarre le 1er novembre (option 3).

Exercice 2 — B2-M3-L6-I2 (C2, B2.2)

Travail en sous-groupe (6 minutes) : lisez cet article et répondez aux questions. Comparez ensuite vos justifications.

Why the shortage of science teachers is a business problem

It is tempting to see the shortage of qualified science and engineering teachers as a matter for education ministries alone. That would be a mistake. Across much of Europe, vacancies for physics and chemistry teachers in secondary schools have doubled in a decade, and vocational colleges report similar difficulties in recruiting instructors for electrical and mechanical courses. The companies that will employ tomorrow's technicians are, in the long run, among the biggest losers.

The causes are well known. Salaries in teaching have not kept pace with those in industry, and an engineer who moves into teaching may take a pay cut of a third or more. Workload, rather than pay, is the reason most often given by teachers who leave the profession early, however, and this suggests that higher salaries alone would not solve the problem.

Some firms have started to act. Ferrand Industrial Systems, a mid-sized automation company, allows its engineers to teach one day a week at a local college while remaining on full pay. The scheme is small – eleven engineers so far – but the college reports that pass rates on the relevant courses have improved, and the company says it has recruited six apprentices it would not otherwise have met.

Critics argue that such schemes are little more than public relations and that they cannot replace properly trained teachers. They are partly right: an engineer teaching one day a week is no substitute for a full-time colleague who knows how to manage a class. Yet the alternative, for many colleges, is not a better-qualified teacher but no teacher at all. Businesses that complain about skills shortages should consider whether they can afford to stay on the sidelines.

1. What is the author's main argument?
A. Education ministries should double teachers' salaries.
B. Vocational colleges should recruit more engineers full-time.
C. Companies have a direct interest in solving the shortage.
D. The shortage of science teachers has been exaggerated.

2. Why does the author think higher salaries alone would not be enough?
A. Teachers who leave early mainly mention workload.
B. Industry salaries are falling.
C. Engineers do not want to teach.
D. Ministries cannot afford higher salaries.

3. What benefit has Ferrand Industrial Systems obtained from its scheme?
A. Lower salary costs for its engineers
B. Public funding for its training centre
C. A full-time teaching post at the college
D. Contact with apprentices it later recruited

4. How does the author respond to the critics of such schemes?
A. He rejects their view completely.
B. He partly agrees but still supports the schemes.
C. He agrees that the schemes are mainly public relations.
D. He says the critics are full-time teachers.

Corrigé
